title: Hasan's peace
hook: Hasan makes a treaty with Mu'awiyah to stop the bloodshed, as the Prophet ﷺ foretold (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ali's death. Struck at prayer in Kufa, he asked that his attacker be dealt with fairly. Your line was fair to his killer.

A boy sits beside his grandfather on the pulpit in Medina. The grandfather is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. He looks out at the people, then at the boy, then at the people again, and says: this son of mine is a sayyid, a leader, and perhaps through him God will make peace between two great groups of Muslims. Bukhari keeps the scene. The boy is Hasan, Ali's elder son. Years later, after his father's death, Hasan stands at the head of an army facing another army.
screen: `A BOY ON THE PULPIT.` → `THIS SON OF MINE IS A LEADER.` → `TWO GREAT GROUPS.`

segments.voice: Bukhari keeps the second scene too, in the words of a later narrator, al-Hasan al-Basri. Hasan leads armies he describes as like mountains. Facing him are the forces of Mu'awiyah, the governor of Syria. One of Mu'awiyah's advisers says these armies will not turn back until each has destroyed the other. And Mu'awiyah asks: if these kill those and those kill these, who will be left to look after the people, their families, their affairs? So he sends two men to Hasan, to talk. Hasan listens, and agrees to step aside and make peace. The histories report conditions in the treaty and differ about the details, so the details are best left to them. Bukhari's narrator ties the outcome straight back to the pulpit: through this son, God might make peace between two great groups. Both groups are Muslims. That is what makes the moment heavy. After the Camel and Siffin, believers against believers, a grandson of the Prophet gives up a claim rather than add to the graves. Muslims remember this differently, and fairly. Shia Muslims honor Hasan as the second Imam, and read the treaty as a wise and costly choice made to protect the believers when war would only have destroyed them. Sunni Muslims honor Hasan as a member of the Prophet's household and a companion, and point to this hadith as the Prophet's own praise of what he did. Tradition calls that year the year of unity. The story that began with Ali as caliph ends not on a battlefield, but with a treaty.
screen: `ARMIES LIKE MOUNTAINS.` · `WHO WILL BE LEFT TO CARE FOR THE PEOPLE?` · `HASAN STEPS ASIDE.` · `BOTH GROUPS ARE MUSLIMS.` · then, large: `PEACE BETWEEN TWO GROUPS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one standing argument where you are, quite possibly, right. Ask Mu'awiyah's question: if this goes on, who is left to look after the people in between, the kids, the team, the friends caught in the middle? Hold the claim in an open hand, and see what it would cost to set it down.
Hasan's peace. A grandson of the Prophet who could have fought, and instead stepped aside so two groups of Muslims would stop killing each other. Today's word.
Your line: peace between two groups. A costly choice, and remembered with love. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims recall Hasan's treaty with Mu'awiyah through the hadith in Bukhari in which the Prophet calls Hasan a leader through whom God may make peace between two groups of Muslims; Shia Muslims honor Hasan as the second Imam.

chat.says: Why did Hasan make peace instead of fighting Mu'awiyah?
options: To stop Muslims killing Muslims, as the Prophet said he might.
Mu'awiyah had already won the battle and captured him.
He wanted to rule from Damascus instead of Kufa.
chat.meaning: Both armies were Muslims. Bukhari's narrator ties Hasan's peace to the Prophet's words: through this son, God might make peace between two great groups.

sayyid.meaning: a leader; the Prophet's word for the boy Hasan

al-Hasan al-Basri.meaning: a later narrator whose words Bukhari keeps

Mu'awiyah.meaning: the governor of Syria, facing Hasan's army
